passage:
Zubin, you call your mentor before choosing a shirt. Sit down. Your Nirmala aunty was worse.

At twenty-four I joined a publishing house, and Mrs. Anand took me under her wing. She was so wise that I stopped thinking. Which manuscript to read first? I asked her. Whether to take a day off? I asked her. Once I even asked which pen to buy.

One day she was away in Delhi, and a writer called wanting an answer on his contract by evening. I sat there frozen, sweating, terrified of choosing wrong.

When Mrs. Anand came back, I expected praise for waiting. Instead she said, very gently, "Nirmala, I don't want to be your brain. I want to be your sounding board."

That was the turning point. From then on I made small decisions myself and brought her only the big ones, with my own view first. "Here's what I think. What am I missing?" She smiled every time.

qa.q: Where was Mrs. Anand when the writer called?
qa.a: She was away in Delhi.

qa.q: How did young Nirmala feel when she had to answer the writer alone?
qa.a: She felt frozen and terrified, sweating with fear of choosing wrong.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Nirmala's story?
qa.a: Mrs. Anand told her she wanted to be a sounding board, not her brain, so Nirmala began making small decisions herself and bringing her own view first.

qa.q: How did Mrs. Anand seem to feel about Nirmala's dependence?
qa.a: Mrs. Anand seemed gently concerned, wanting Nirmala to trust her own judgment rather than rely on her for everything.

grounding: An elder's story shows a young woman who asked her mentor to decide everything out of fear of mistakes, and who learned to take small decisions and ask for perspective, not answers.

The vendor needed an answer by four, and Suraj, Vaibhav's mentor, was on a flight to Singapore with his phone off. Vaibhav stared at the two quotes on his screen. For a year he had run every decision past Suraj: which supplier, which font, which reply. He had never once gone first.

His palms were damp. What if he picked the wrong one and cost the company?

He made himself do what Suraj always did. He wrote down price, delivery time, and past quality for both vendors. The cheaper one had missed two deadlines last year. The other was slightly more expensive but reliable.

At three-forty he signed with the reliable one and emailed Suraj: "Chose Vendor B for reliability; here's my reasoning. Would you have done anything differently?"

Suraj replied that night from the airport. "Same choice. Next time, don't even ask me. Just tell me." Vaibhav read it three times, grinning.

qa.q: Where was Suraj flying to?
qa.a: Suraj was flying to Singapore.

qa.q: What was Vaibhav feeling as he looked at the two quotes?
qa.a: Vaibhav felt anxious, with damp palms, afraid of choosing wrong and costing the company.

qa.q: What did Vaibhav do instead of waiting for Suraj?
qa.a: He weighed the options using Suraj's method, made the decision himself, and asked Suraj for perspective afterwards rather than for the answer.

qa.q: How did Suraj feel about Vaibhav's decision?
qa.a: Suraj was pleased and trusting, telling Vaibhav he no longer needed to ask first.

grounding: The story shows a young man who asked his mentor to decide everything out of fear of mistakes, who takes a decision himself and asks for perspective, building trust in his own judgment.

passage:
You asked why I went quiet last month. I'm Amandeep, and my ex Ayesha messaged me. "Found our old playlist. Thinking of you."

I'm not proud of it, but my heart went wild. For two days I replayed everything: the Ludhiana rooftop, her laugh, road trips. I nearly typed "Let's meet." I remembered her as perfect.

Then my sister asked, "Bhaiya, what exactly do you miss?" I thought hard. The rooftop. The songs. Being someone's person. And then, because she made me, I remembered why it ended. Ayesha hated my job. She called me boring in front of friends. We fought every Sunday. I'd left out all the Sundays.

I realised I wasn't missing Ayesha as she was. I was lonely, and I was missing a feeling.

So I wrote back, kindly: "That playlist was great. I hope you're well. I don't think we should go back." Then I called my cousins and planned a weekend trip.

qa.q: What did Ayesha's message say?
qa.a: It said, "Found our old playlist. Thinking of you."

qa.q: What did Amandeep feel when the message arrived?
qa.a: Amandeep felt a wild rush of longing, replaying old memories and nearly suggesting they meet.

qa.q: Which question helped Amandeep choose wisely, and why?
qa.a: His sister asking what exactly he missed made him separate the feeling from the real relationship and remember why it ended.

qa.q: How might Ayesha feel reading Amandeep's reply?
qa.a: Ayesha may feel disappointed but respected, since the reply was kind and clear.

grounding: A spoken account shows a young man whose ex messages him, whose old feelings surge with polished memories, and who asks what he truly misses and chooses consciously.

Sunday night. Tanya's message came at eleven: "Saw a man selling roasted corn and thought of you. Miss you." Suraj sat up in bed. Eight months since the breakup. His chest ached with a sudden longing. He opened their old photos: Juhu beach, the scooter trip to Lonavala, her head on his shoulder. He fell asleep with the phone in his hand.

Wednesday. At lunch he told Imran, his oldest friend. "I think I should meet her." Imran put down his fork. "Remember the Lonavala trip? She didn't speak to you for two days because you were ten minutes late." Suraj had forgotten that. He'd also forgotten the jealous calls, the tears when he met his friends.

The next Monday. Suraj had thought about it all week. He missed being loved; he didn't miss being afraid of her moods. He replied: "I'm glad you're okay. I don't want to restart things, but I wish you well." Then he joined Imran's Saturday football team.

passage:
At the university counselling centre, Yamini sat with her phone face up on her knee. On the screen was a post she'd drafted at 2 a.m.: screenshots of her ex Karan's messages, the ones where he mocked her weight to his friends while they were still together.

"I want everyone to see who he is," she said. Her jaw was tight.

Nirmala, the counsellor, didn't argue. "What he did was wrong. Your anger makes sense."

Yamini's eyes filled. "It's been a year. Why am I still this angry?"

"What would posting it give you?"

Yamini thought. "Five minutes of feeling powerful. Then a week of his friends commenting. Then I'd still be thinking about him."

"So what might help, instead?"

They talked about writing an unsent letter, and about her friends, who had been asking to help. Yamini deleted the draft in front of Nirmala. Her hands shook a little. "Next Thursday, same time?" "Same time."

qa.q: What had Karan mocked in his messages?
qa.a: He had mocked her weight to his friends.

qa.q: What was Yamini feeling as she described the post?
qa.a: Yamini felt a tight, lasting anger at Karan, and confusion about why it hadn't faded after a year.

qa.q: Why did Yamini delete the revenge post?
qa.a: She saw it would give only brief power and keep her tied to Karan, so she chose counselling, an unsent letter and her friends' support instead.

qa.q: How does Nirmala respond to Yamini's anger?
qa.a: Nirmala accepts the anger as fair and acknowledges the wrong, then helps Yamini find ways to heal without revenge.

grounding: The passage shows a young woman still angry at how her ex treated her, who acknowledges the wrong, seeks counselling and friends' support and avoids a revenge post.

passage:
Dear Aadhya,

I'm writing to say thank you for Saturday night, when you took my phone away.

You know what I was about to send Nikhil. Three paragraphs about exactly what kind of person cheats on someone for a year and then tells everyone she was "too needy". Every word was true. I was shaking with rage.

You didn't tell me I was wrong to be angry. You said, "He did a horrible thing. And every message you send him keeps him in your life."

I couldn't sleep, but by morning I knew you were right. Two years after the breakup and I'm still spending my evenings on him.

So here's what I've done. I've booked a session with a counsellor my cousin recommended, for Wednesday. I've deleted the draft. I've muted him everywhere. And I'm coming to your pottery class on Sunday.

Thank you for being the friend who says the hard thing.

Love,
Reena

Monday, the first week. Binita had ended it with Anirban on Saturday. By Monday he had sent forty messages: "Just talk to me." "You owe me that." She replied to some, trying to be kind. Each reply brought ten more. She felt uneasy, checking her phone every few minutes.

The following Monday. Binita wrote one message, read it to her friend Shreya first, and sent it: "Anirban, it's over. Please don't contact me again. I won't be replying." Then she blocked him, saved screenshots of every message with dates, and told her flatmates, her parents and her team lead at work.

Two weeks later. Anirban was waiting outside her office gate at six. Binita's heart pounded. She didn't stop or speak. She went back inside and told the security guard, who walked her to her cab. That evening, with her father beside her, she took her screenshots to the police station and filed a complaint. The officer took it seriously.

qa.q: How many messages had Anirban sent by Monday?
qa.a: He had sent forty messages.

qa.q: How did Binita feel as the messages kept coming?
qa.a: Binita felt uneasy and on edge, checking her phone every few minutes.

qa.q: What steps did Binita take to protect herself?
qa.a: She sent one clear final message, stopped engaging, blocked him, kept dated records, told trusted people, and went to the police when he turned up.

qa.q: How did Shreya help Binita?

passage:
Madhav, you think only girls get followed around by an ex? Let your Vikas mama tell you what happened to me at twenty-four.

When I ended things with Rhea, she didn't accept it. First it was calls, thirty a day. Then she started turning up at my office canteen. Then outside my rented room at night, knocking.

I felt uneasy all the time, and embarrassed. Who would believe a man was scared?

My turning point was my elder brother. He said, "Being scared is not weakness. Stop answering her. Say it once, clearly, and then write everything down."

So I sent one message: "Rhea, it's over. Please do not contact me or come here again." After that, nothing. I noted every call and visit in a diary with dates. I told my landlord, my manager and my brother.

When she came at midnight a week later, my brother came with me to the police station the next morning. They spoke to her family. It stopped.

qa.q: How many calls a day did Rhea make at first?
qa.a: She made thirty calls a day.

qa.q: How did young Vikas feel while Rhea kept turning up?
qa.a: He felt uneasy all the time and embarrassed, worried nobody would believe a man could be scared.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Vikas's story?
qa.a: His brother told him being scared wasn't weakness, so he gave one clear final message, stopped responding, kept records, told trusted people and went to the police.

qa.q: How did Vikas's brother see the situation?
qa.a: His brother took it seriously as a safety problem and stayed by Vikas's side through the steps.

grounding: An elder's story shows a young man whose ex kept calling and turning up after he ended it, who gave one clear final boundary, stopped engaging, kept records, told trusted people and went to the police.

A Tuesday in January. Scrolling late, Vasudha saw it: Sameer's wedding photo. Five years since he left her with two weeks' notice before their engagement. Her chest tightened with the old bitterness, and she was surprised by how tired she felt of it. She closed the app.

The next Saturday. Over coffee, her colleague Lalremsiami told her about forgiving her own father. "It wasn't for him. I just wanted my evenings back." That night Vasudha wrote a page in her journal: what Sameer had done, how much it had hurt, and at the bottom, "I'm done carrying this." She didn't send anything. She didn't need to.

Six weeks later. At a friend's baby shower, Sameer was there with his wife. Vasudha's heart jumped once. Then she walked over. "Congratulations on the wedding. I wish you both well." He looked startled. "Thank you. I... thank you." She went back to the cake table. She felt light, and a little amazed.

qa.q: How much notice had Sameer given before their engagement?
qa.a: He had given two weeks' notice.

qa.q: What did Vasudha feel when she saw the wedding photo?
qa.a: Vasudha felt old bitterness tighten her chest, and a surprising tiredness of carrying it.

Arnab, you ask why I'm smiling at this old photo? That's Bimal. I was engaged to him at twenty-three. Your Ishita dida has a story.

Three months before the wedding, he broke it off by letter. No reason. My father had already printed the cards. For years I couldn't hear his name without my hands going cold. I told myself I'd forgive him only when he apologised.

He never did.

When I was twenty-six, I saw him at the Durga puja pandal with his wife and a small boy. I expected rage. Instead I felt tired of the weight. That night was my turning point. I decided I would forgive him, for my sake, not his. No letter, no apology needed.

The next year I saw him again, by the sweet stall. I said, "Bimal, I hold nothing against you. Be well." He looked stunned. I walked away and bought rosogolla for your grandfather.

I never went back to that story again.

qa.q: How did Bimal break off the engagement?
qa.a: He broke it off by letter, with no reason.

qa.q: How did young Ishita feel for years after the engagement ended?
qa.a: She felt hurt and resentful, her hands going cold at his name, waiting for an apology.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Ishita's story?

qa.q: How might Bimal have felt when Ishita spoke to him?

In their Dadar flat, Bhavna was carefully planning the Saturday grocery list, and Vijay caught himself thinking about Ritika. Ritika, who used to wake him at midnight to drive to Marine Drive for chai. Ritika, who never made lists.

It kept happening. Bhavna suggested a quiet dinner; he thought, Ritika would have picked a rooftop party. He felt restless and vaguely dissatisfied, and then guilty.

One evening he remembered, sharply, the other side of Ritika: cancelled plans, the months when she didn't call, the night he waited three hours at the station. His memory had kept only the midnight chai.

Bhavna came in with two cups. She had noticed his headache and made ginger tea without being asked. He looked at her properly for the first time in weeks.

"Bhavna, can I say something? I love how steady you are. And sometimes I miss doing something unplanned. Could we try one surprise evening a month?"

She laughed. "I'll put it on the list."

"You're quiet again," Shreya said, sitting beside Mohit on the sofa.

"Just tired."

"Mohit."

He sighed. "Okay. This is going to sound bad. Sometimes I compare you with Sonam."

Shreya went still. "Go on."

"She and I used to talk for hours about books. You and I mostly talk about work and your mother's knee. And I start thinking, it was better then."

"Was it?"

Mohit paused. "No. That's the thing. I remember the book talks. I forget she mocked my job, and that we broke up because she never wanted to plan anything with me. I'm comparing you with the good bits of her."

Shreya exhaled slowly. "That hurt to hear. But thank you for being honest."

"You're kinder than she was. You show up. I just miss real conversations sometimes."

"Then let's have them. Sunday mornings, no phones. You pick the first book."

He smiled, relieved. "Deal."

The community hall in Wakad was full of fairy lights for Pooja's wedding reception. Jahnavi was laughing with her college friends by the dessert counter when she saw him: Kunal, her ex, by the stage, in a navy kurta.

Her stomach flipped. They hadn't spoken since the breakup a year ago. Her friends were watching her, and she felt the urge to laugh louder, look busier, prove something.

She didn't. When their paths crossed near the photo booth, she said, "Hi, Kunal. Good to see you."

"Hi, Jahnavi. You look well."

"Thanks. Pooja looks so happy, doesn't she?"

"She does."

"Enjoy the evening." She moved on to her friends.

It had taken thirty seconds. Her heart was still racing, but nothing had exploded. Her friend Tina squeezed her arm. "Very classy." Jahnavi laughed, properly this time, and went back for another gulab jamun.

passage:
Hi Megha,

You asked how the wedding went. Short version: Kunal was there.

I walked into the hall and there he was, at the same table as Sonal and Rishi. Our first time in the same room since the breakup. My hands went cold. For a second I thought about leaving.

I didn't. I decided on three rules in the car park: say hello, keep it short, don't act.

So when he came over, I said, "Hi, Kunal. How's the new job?" He said good. I said, "Nice," and turned to Sonal's mother to admire her saree. That was it. No dramatic laughter, no cold shoulder.

The weird thing? By the dessert I'd almost forgotten he was there. I danced with the bride's cousins and came home tired and fine.

I think it gets easier every time. And I have a whole new life now; that helps.

Call me on Sunday?

Ishita

qa.a: He was sitting at the same table as Sonal and Rishi.

In Lisbon, on the tram to work, Siddiq saw the photo: Inês, his ex, laughing on a beach in the Algarve, with a tall man's arm around her. The caption said "Happy". Something sharp twisted in his chest. Jealousy, hot and stupid.

He clicked on the man's profile. Then stopped, thumb hovering. If he went down this path, he'd spend the evening scrolling strangers' holidays.

He locked the phone and looked out of the window. He reminded himself: he had ended it. They had wanted different lives. She wanted to move back to Porto; he wanted to stay. That was still true.

That evening Paulo, his flatmate, found him cooking. "You okay? You look like someone stole your bike."

"Saw Inês is seeing someone."

"Ah. Want to talk?"

"No. I want to finish this pasta and sign up for that climbing class."

Paulo grinned. "Then sign me up too."

She took her plate to the far side. Her colleague Noor slid in opposite. "You've gone pale."

In the small town of Chhindwara, Lokesh picked up his daughter Guddi every Friday from his ex-wife Sunita's house, and every Friday they fought. About Guddi's tuition. About the time. About nothing.

This Friday Guddi, six, handed him a folded note at the gate. "Mummy says give this to you." It said: "Tell your father her school fees are due." Lokesh's jaw tightened. He started writing a reply to send back with Guddi.

Then he saw his daughter's face, watching him, worried.

He crumpled the paper into his pocket instead. "Chalo, Guddi. Ice cream."

That night, he called his friend Nilesh, who had been through a divorce. "Keep it short, keep it about her, and never through her," Nilesh said.

On Sunday Lokesh sent Sunita a text. "Fees paid today. From now on, let's message each other directly about school things, not through Guddi. Tuition timings: shall we talk Tuesday?" Sunita replied: "Okay. Tuesday."

qa.q: How old was Guddi?

qa.q: What was Lokesh feeling when he read the note?
qa.a: Lokesh felt a tight flash of anger, then concern when he saw Guddi looking worried.

qa.q: What might Guddi feel carrying notes between her parents?
qa.a: Guddi likely feels worried and caught in the middle, as her face at the gate showed.

passage:
Olga and Marek had been divorced for a year, and in their small city outside Kraków, every handover of their daughter Ada ended in a quarrel on the pavement. This Sunday it was about a missing mitten.

"You never pack properly," Olga snapped.

"And you never let me finish a sentence," Marek shot back.

Ada, five, stood between them in her pink coat, looking at the ground. Then she said, very quietly, "Can I go inside?"

Olga felt as if someone had slapped her. She saw it suddenly from Ada's height: two giants shouting over her head, every week.

She took a breath. "Marek, I'm sorry. Let's not do this here. We'll write to each other about her things, not argue at the door."

He blinked, then nodded. "Okay. Good."

They kept it up. Handovers became two minutes: a hug, a bag, "Bye, see you Wednesday." Ada began to skip up the steps.

qa.q: What was the quarrel about this Sunday?
qa.a: It was about a missing mitten.

qa.q: How did Olga feel when Ada asked to go inside?
qa.a: Olga felt stung and ashamed, as if slapped, seeing the quarrels from Ada's point of view.

qa.q: What changed about Olga and Marek's handovers?
qa.a: They agreed to discuss Ada's needs in writing instead of arguing at the door, keeping handovers short, calm and focused on her.

qa.q: How was Ada affected by her parents' quarrels?
qa.a: Ada felt caught in the middle and unhappy, looking at the ground, and later skipped up the steps once the fights stopped.

grounding: The passage shows a young mother who shares a child with her ex and keeps fighting, who chooses short, respectful, child-focused contact so her daughter's stability comes first.

"Mummy, the hostel is only forty minutes away. I'll come home every Sunday."

Indu pressed a hand to her chest. "Go, then. My BP is already high. If something happens to me at night, who will know?"

"Mummy, you have Papa, and Mrs. Joshi next door."

"Papa doesn't notice anything. You're my only daughter." A long silence. Then: "I suppose I didn't raise you right."

Deepika's throat tightened. The old guilt rose, the one that always ended with her unpacking her bag.

"Mummy, I love you. It's not about you. The night shifts at the hospital end at two. I can't travel home safely at that hour."

I'm Jahnavi, and until last year, my mother Aparna's silence ran my life.

Whenever I made a choice she didn't like, Amma just stopped speaking. When I chose commerce instead of medicine, eleven days. When I cut my hair short, four days. When I said I wanted to take the job in Hyderabad, she didn't speak to me for three weeks, and I felt like the worst daughter alive.

I kept apologising for wanting things.

My friend's aunt, who is a counsellor, said something that changed how I saw it: "Silence used to punish isn't love. And it isn't your fault."

So when the Hyderabad offer came again, I didn't wait for Amma's permission. I told her gently, "Amma, I'm taking it. I'll call you every Sunday." She went silent. I kept calling every Sunday anyway, talking even when she didn't answer.

In the seventh week, she said, "Are you eating properly?" It was a start. I also began seeing a counsellor myself.

qa.q: How many days did Amma stop speaking when Jahnavi cut her hair short?
qa.a: She stopped speaking for four days.

qa.q: How did Jahnavi feel during Amma's three weeks of silence?
qa.a: Jahnavi felt guilty, like the worst daughter alive, and kept apologising for wanting things.

qa.q: How did Jahnavi set a gentle, firm boundary?
qa.a: She told Amma kindly she was taking the job, kept calling every Sunday regardless of the silence, and sought support from a counsellor.

qa.q: How might Aparna experience the Sunday calls?
qa.a: She may feel hurt and resistant at first, but slowly softens, as her question about eating properly shows.

grounding: A first-person account shows a young woman whose mother controls her with silence, who recognises it is not love or her fault, sets a gentle firm boundary, keeps warmth and seeks support.
